Concept map: from text to inference Slide 4

Slide 4 writes text-as-data research as a chain: corpus → representation → model → validation → inference. Click each step for an explanation (the explanations are organized from slide 4; the examples are supplementary):

→ → → →
  • Corpus: e.g., parliamentary speeches, party manifestos, court rulings, news, tweets, open-ended survey responses.Slide 3
  • Representation: bag of words, word embeddings, language models.Slide 4
  • Model: dictionaries, classifiers, topic models, scaling.Slide 4
  • Validation: comparison with human coding, expert judgment, external benchmarks.Slide 4
  • Inference: use what you measured to answer a social science question; "the social science question is the job."Slide 4

01 · Part 1

Why text? What is text as data

In this chapter
Why textDefinitionRepresentation: bag of wordsInteractive: bag-of-words builderSelf-check

Why text? Slide 3

The starting point of slide 3: most political activity leaves a textual or digital trace.

Where texts come from (Slide 3)
  • Parliamentary speeches, hearing transcripts, party manifestos
  • Court rulings, bills, administrative records, diplomatic cables
  • News reports, social media posts, politicians' tweets
  • Open-ended survey responses, interview transcripts
Then vs. now (Slide 3)

Then: human reading and hand coding (e.g., the Manifesto Project).

Now: scale: millions of documents can be analyzed systematically.

Benoit (2020) opens in a similar way: legislative debates, manifestos, committee transcripts, speeches, lobbying documents, court opinions and laws are not only recorded today, but many are in forms that are easy to turn into structured data (Benoit 2020, repo PDF p. 2).

What is "Text as Data"? Slide 4

Definition (Slide 4): treating text as data: turning unstructured language/data into quantitative information that can be analyzed, in order to answer social science questions.

Slide 4 also lists common options at three stages of the pipeline:

StageOptions listed on slide 4Roughly which weeks of this course (from syllabus schedule titles; supplement)
Representationbag of words, word embeddings, language modelsW4 (tokenisation, DFM), W9 (embeddings), W10, W12 (transformers, LLMs)
Modeldictionaries, classifiers, topic models, scalingW4 (dictionaries), W6 (classification), W7 (scaling), W8 (topic models)
Validationcomparison with human coding, expert judgment, external benchmarksAppears every week

The first step of representation: bag of words

This week's slides only name "bag of words"; the details come in W4. Here we borrow Grimmer & Stewart (2013) to build intuition: when turning text into numbers, the most consequential and most surprising step is discarding word order, assuming documents are a "bag of words". The authors argue that examples where word order changes the meaning of a sentence are rare in practice, and unigrams alone usually suffice to convey the gist of a text; if that is unacceptable, bigrams and trigrams can be added to retain some word order (Grimmer & Stewart 2013, p. 272).

They also warn that all quantitative models of language are wrong. Their example is the classic joke "Time flies like an arrow. Fruit flies like a banana.": the same "flies like" is a metaphor in the first half and literal in the second (p. 270). A bag of words cannot see this difference at all.

Interactive: bag-of-words builder Slide 4

🧺Toy demo: throwing sentences into a bag of wordsSupplement (not from the lecture)

Type a document (in English) in each box; the document-feature matrix below updates instantly. The tokenization rule is a simplified version written for these notes (splitting on spaces and punctuation), not quanteda's rule; quanteda's real results are in chapter 11.

Try "Example: swapped word order": the two sentences mean opposite things but are identical in a unigram bag of words; only after ticking bigrams can they be told apart. This is the trade-off Grimmer & Stewart describe.

“Validation is the one demand that never went away.” Slide 5

This sentence is one of the most important messages of the week. Grimmer & Stewart's (2013) fourth principle is "Validate, Validate, Validate" (Table 1, p. 269); Baden et al. (2022) surveyed authors of text-analysis studies and found that 40% saw validity as a major concern and another 35% as a minor concern (p. 6). In the era of LLMs as annotators, the question is still: does what the model labels match the concept you want to measure?

In plain words (supplement)

The tools keep changing: word counts, topics, vectors, LLMs. But every generation of researchers has to answer the same question: "How do you know you measured the thing you say you measured?"

Mapping to the textbook Slides 6, 12

The textbook Grimmer, Roberts & Stewart (2022) divides the work into three tasks: discovery, measurement, inference. This course merges them into two: measurement ≈ discovery + measurement; application ≈ inference.Slide 6 The book is the framework for the lectures, but you do not need to buy it; the course is paper-based, with 3–4 core readings per week, and excerpts of required book chapters will be provided.Slide 12

04 · Part 1

Two research cases: From Pork to Policy, and turning open-ended answers into causal maps

In this chapter
Case 1: Catalinac (2016)Case 2: Jankin, Liao & Tang (2026)Interactive: causal mapsInteractive: κ and F1Self-check

Case 1: From Pork to Policy Slide 7

Catalinac (2016), The Journal of Politics 78(1): 1–18. Slide 7 focuses on the role of the method:

  • Method: an off-the-shelf tool, not a new one: LDA (2003), with every topic validated by reading.
  • The contribution is political science, not a new algorithm.
  • Building new NLP models is the job of computer science; our job is to use them well to answer a question.Slide 7

Slide 7 shows a screenshot of the paper's abstract; W1's papers/ folder does not contain the full text, so these notes do not summarize the paper's content or numbers. This paper reappears in W8 (topic models).

Case 2: coding open-ended answers as causal maps Slides 8–9

Research design (Slide 8)
  • Jankin, Liao & Tang (2026), Folk Theories of Partisan Conflict (working paper)
  • Question: does what a partisan believes about "why the country is divided" matter beyond how much they dislike the other side?
  • Data: 1,200 US adults (quota-matched); several open-ended questions (the figure on the slide codes Q7).
The prompt (Slide 8, original wording)

“Which factors, events, groups, or institutions do you think caused Democrats and Republicans to view each other more negatively than they did 50 years ago? Please explain what caused what, who or what you think was responsible, and what effects followed.”

The key measurement step (Slide 8): code each free-text answer as a directed acyclic graph (DAG): nodes are the factors the respondent mentions (15 factors, 3 domains), and edges are the causal links they draw.
  • Same factors, opposite arrows: only the direction separates the two theories; the graph gives each person's root cause.Slide 9
  • Validation: coder agreement on "which factors each answer mentions" κ = 0.84; an LLM using the same codebook compared with human coding F1 = 0.92.Slide 9
  • What the text does: the theory you hold predicts your tolerance of anti-democratic actions, even after controlling for affective polarization (affect) and ideology.Slide 9

The figure on slide 9 (Fig. 4) shows common folk theories grouped by root cause (% = share within party); these notes do not transcribe the figure's numbers, so see the slide on the right. This is a working paper; the repo has no full text.

Course positioning, materials and the 16-week schedule

In this chapter
Who this course is forWhere the materials come fromThree blocksInteractive: scheduleSelf-check

Who is this course for? Slide 11

A social science course, not a technology course.Slide 11

This is an introductory course designed for students of the Graduate Institute of National Development and related social science fields, and it requires no advanced technical training; the focus is on using text-as-data and NLP techniques to answer substantive research questions in political science, political communication, legal studies, sociology and similar fields.

  • Want to learn model internals, architectures, optimization? This is not that course.
  • Goal: use these methods to write your own political science / social science paper.Slide 11

Where the materials come from Slide 12

  • Lecture framework: Grimmer, Roberts & Stewart (2022), Text as Data: A New Framework for Machine Learning and the Social Sciences (Princeton University Press). This course's two kinds of work simplify the book's discovery → measurement → inference.
  • No need to buy the book: the course is paper-first, with 3–4 core materials per week, mostly journal articles and open tutorials; excerpts of required book chapters are provided.
  • Also useful: Benoit (2020), Nielbo et al. (2024), Watanabe & Müller's quanteda tutorials, Jurafsky & Martin's SLP (free online).Slide 12

The semester in three blocks Slide 14

W1–W2 · Foundations

Introduction to quantitative text analysis; text preparation and a collaborative R/Python workflow.

W4–W8 · Core methods

Tokenisation and DFMs; dictionaries and sentiment analysis; human coding and classification; scaling; topic models.

W9–W13 · Advanced representations

Readability, similarity and embeddings; NLP and transformers; LLMs; multilingual and multimodal data.

No class: W3 (9/25), W5 (10/9), W11 (11/20), W16 (12/25).Slide 14

Before the course: R, Python, IDE, GitHub, Overleaf

In this chapter
Languages and packagesIDE and writing toolsGitHub and OverleafWeekly workloadInteractive: setup checklistSelf-check

Languages and packages Slide 15

This course requires prior experience with R and the ability to run some code in a Python environment; beyond that, no advanced technical training is needed.

R: most of the course and methods

quanteda, tidytext, text2vec, udpipe, keyATM, spacyr

Python: optional

transformers, flair (transformer models); gensim, spacy (NLP tools); BERTopic (topic models)

Please bring a laptop with a working development environment already installed: most sessions are a short lecture plus coding exercises you run yourself. A detailed setup guide will be sent before the first class.Slide 15

IDE and writing tools Slide 16

  • IDE: RStudio for R; Positron for Python and cross-language work. You should be able to edit and run code, debug, manage packages and use the built-in terminal.
  • R Markdown / Quarto (RStudio) and Jupyter / Quarto notebooks (Positron) help but are not required; W2 covers the actual setup and workflow.
  • Never used these IDEs? Complete a basic tutorial before W2, so the semester is spent on methods, not fighting tools.
  • Written assignments and posters use LaTeX, done in shared Overleaf projects; Quarto can be used for analysis notebooks. Optional: possibly LM Studio to run LLaMA or Mistral locally, with no API costs.Slide 16

GitHub for code, Overleaf for written work Slide 17

  • Course materials (slides, code, data, exercises) are all on GitHub. Keep research code in a private repository.
  • Written assignments are submitted through shared Overleaf projects, with edit access for the instructor.
  • Create a free GitHub account and install GitHub Desktop (point-and-click, no command line needed); RStudio and Positron also have built-in Git tools.
  • Apply for the free GitHub Student Developer Pack (GitHub Pro, Copilot, etc.) with your university email.
  • W1: how course rules and materials, assignments and communication are organized; W2: GitHub Desktop and IDE setup (clone, commit, sharing code).Slide 17
Extra details from the syllabus (syllabus §8.1, syllabus PDF p. 39)

Use a separate Overleaf project for each graded assignment, named with your name and the assignment; before the deadline invite the instructor as Editor (can edit); view-only access does not count as a submission. The project must contain the complete, up-to-date source files and compile successfully to PDF. A free account allows one collaborator per project, which is enough.

Self-paced coding exercises and class participation Slide 19

  • Lab files provide examples and exercises. These exercises are not graded and do not need to be submitted.
  • Class Participation — 20%: taking part in discussions of readings, methods and applications; peer feedback; questions and answers on NTU COOL or the course GitHub Issues.
  • Written assignments and posters are made in LaTeX and submitted through shared Overleaf projects.Slide 19

Final poster presentation — 25% Slides 20–21

  • W15 poster session: first a 5-minute introduction of your poster, then discussion and peer feedback; stay by your poster for the whole session to answer questions; other faculty may be invited.
  • Posters follow the PolMeth poster guidelines: clear visual design, emphasizing the research question, data and methods, main findings and implications.
  • W14 is a poster preparation workshop (format, visual presentation, 5-minute talk), counted toward class participation.Slide 20
  • Slide 21 shows four PolMeth 2025 posters as examples (Atsusaka, Lee & Lee; Jeon; Xia, Zeng, Liao & Jankin; Li); compare their research questions, evidence and visual organization.Slide 21

Two papers Slides 22–23

Midterm research design report — 20% (Slide 22)

Your own research or thesis topic, done individually. The research set up in the midterm report is completed by the final paper.

  • Abstract
  • Introduction: question and motivation
  • Literature review: positioning the research
  • Research design: data, methods, strategy
  • Preliminary results, or the planned analysis strategy
  • Feasibility, expected findings, contribution

At most 10 pages and no more than 2,500 words. Due: December 4 (W13).

Final paper — 25% (Slide 23)

Also done individually. It continues the midterm report and adds the full empirical analysis: a stronger design, robust inference, appropriate validation and sensitivity checks, followed by findings, limitations and contribution.

  • Main text: at most 4,000 words (excluding references), written as a PSRM Research Note
  • Appendix: no word or page limit (robustness, alternative specifications, validation, annotation procedures, prompts, model details, code documentation)
  • A reproducible code repository (GitHub or CodeOcean)
  • Due: TBA

Where to start? Slide 24

If you do not have a corpus in mind yet, the syllabus lists these suggested topics:

Legislatures and parties
  • Legislative behavior in Taiwan: roll-call votes, speeches, interpellations
  • Analysis of legislative speech
  • Party manifestos (cross-national or over time)
Media and rhetoric
  • Political discourse on social media
  • News framing of political issues
  • Comparative political rhetoric
  • CCP wolf-warrior diplomacy and propaganda

Pick a topic you will still be working on by the W15 poster session.Slide 24

Institutional and geographic names: required for every extra-credit submission Slide 28

  • Use the official name National Taiwan University in the manuscript, submission-system data, cover letter, acknowledgments, slides, posters and any public materials.
  • Do not alter, omit or downgrade the university's name, and do not use wording that disparages or misrepresents Taiwan's status; when a location is needed, use “Taipei, Taiwan” or “Taipei, Taiwan (R.O.C.)”.
  • This does not prohibit evidence-based criticism of Taiwan's politics, institutions or public policy; it governs accurate institutional and geographic description, professional conduct and non-misleading presentation.
  • If a conference, journal, submission system or editor asks you to change the wording of NTU or Taiwan, you must consult the instructor first before proceeding; discussing submission plans with the instructor in advance is also strongly recommended.Slide 28

Generative AI, academic integrity and deadlines

In this chapter
Three rules for using generative AIInteractive: AI disclosure statementAcademic integrityDeadlinesPractice: scenario judgmentsSelf-check

Using generative AI Slide 29

This course follows NTU's guidelines on generative AI use and research integrity. AI is an assistive tool: it does not replace your judgment, nor your responsibility for what you submit.

  1. Permitted uses in assignments: conceptualisation; initial literature screening (must be verified by a human); writing and editing assistance; audiovisual and interactive components. The arguments and analysis must be your own.
  2. Disclose AI use in every submission: research abstract, midterm report, poster, final paper, extra-credit submissions. State which tool and version, what you asked it to do, how you used its output, and how you checked it. No AI used? Write: “No generative AI tools were used in the preparation of this assignment.”
  3. No statement, no acceptance: an assignment without a statement will not be accepted until a complete statement is added. Misrepresenting AI use, failing to verify AI output, fabricating sources or data through AI, or using AI to bypass learning objectives may be treated as academic misconduct.Slide 29

Supplementary lab: turning this week's slides into data (R)

  
Supplement (not from the lecture)
W1 has no classroom or lab R script (the first take-home lab starts in W2). This chapter is a small demo written by the TA: extract the text of week1.pdf with pdftotext -layout, treat one slide page = one document, and use quanteda to walk through the first two steps of slide 4 (corpus → representation). All output comes from actually running the code locally (R 4.5.3 (aarch64-conda-linux-gnu), quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, stopwords 2.3, jsonlite 2.0.0); the full log is in tad/labs/W1/run_output.txt. These functions are formally taught in W2 and W4, so it is fine if you do not follow everything yet.

R · S01 (supplementary script run_W1.R)
# S01 讀檔：一頁投影片＝一份文件
raw <- paste(readLines("tad/work/W1/week1.txt", encoding = "UTF-8", warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
pages <- strsplit(raw, "\f", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
pages <- pages[nchar(trimws(pages)) > 0]
pages <- gsub("\\s*\\d+/38\\s*$", "", pages)   # 去掉頁尾的「N/38」頁碼
length(pages)
part <- ifelse(seq_along(pages) <= 9, "Part 1: Text as Data",
        ifelse(seq_along(pages) <= 34, "Part 2: How This Course Works", "References"))
corp <- corpus(pages, docvars = data.frame(page = seq_along(pages), part = part))
docnames(corp) <- paste0("p", seq_along(pages))
table(docvars(corp, "part"))

38 pages → 38 documents. Following the structure of the slides, they fall into three groups: pages 1–9 Part 1 (page 1 is the cover, page 2 the Part 1 title page), pages 10–34 Part 2, pages 35–38 references. This decision about "what counts as a document" is exactly the researcher's choice at the corpus step of slide 4's pipeline.


  
S02: four preprocessing settings

  
R · S02 (supplementary script run_W1.R)
# S02 切字：四種前處理設定
toks_A <- tokens(corp)                                             # A 只切字
toks_B <- tokens(corp, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE,
                 remove_symbols = TRUE, remove_url = TRUE)         # B 去標點/數字/符號/網址
toks_C <- tokens_remove(tokens_tolower(toks_B), stopwords("en"))   # C 再轉小寫、去停用詞
toks_D <- tokens_wordstem(toks_C, language = "en")                 # D 再取詞幹
cfg <- list(A = toks_A, B = toks_B, C = toks_C, D = toks_D)
data.frame(setting = names(cfg),
           tokens  = sapply(cfg, function(x) sum(ntoken(x))),
           types   = sapply(cfg, function(x) nfeat(dfm(x, tolower = FALSE))))

  
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3 (aarch64-conda-linux-gnu), quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, stopwords 2.3, jsonlite 2.0.0)

> toks_C <- tokens_remove(tokens_tolower(toks_B), stopwords("en"))   # C 再轉小寫、去停用詞

> toks_D <- tokens_wordstem(toks_C, language = "en")                 # D 再取詞幹

> cfg <- list(A = toks_A, B = toks_B, C = toks_C, D = toks_D)

> data.frame(setting = names(cfg),
+            tokens  = sapply(cfg, function(x) sum(ntoken(x))),
+            types   = sapply(cfg, function(x) nfeat(dfm(x, tolower = FALSE))))
  setting tokens types
A       A   4499  1422
B       B   3123  1328
C       C   2215  1061
D       D   2215   896

  

    
tokens
The total number of "words" the text is split into.

    
types
How many distinct words there are (= the number of columns in the DFM).

    
A → B
Remove punctuation, numbers, symbols and URLs: 4,499 → 3,123 tokens.

    
B → C
Lowercase and remove English stopwords: 3,123 → 2,215 tokens; types 1,328 → 1,061.

    
C → D
Stemming: the token count is unchanged (2,215), but types drop from 1,061 to 896, because words like method and methods are merged into one column.

⚖️Keyness: the χ² statisticReal data: output of textstat_keyness

    

      
Right (green) = relatively more frequent in Part 1 (research content); left (red) = relatively more frequent in Part 2 (course rules). With only 9 pages against 25 and very small counts, χ² merely describes differences in word use; do not treat it as a serious statistical test.

      

      
    

  


  
What this small experiment shows

  
    
    
  • Defining a document is the researcher's decision: one page is one document, so the cover, the title page and the reference pages are all "documents" too, and they affect the most frequent words.
    • 
    
  • Preprocessing changes the data: for the same slides, the number of features can be 1,422, 1,328, 1,061 or 896, depending on how you process them. Baden et al. (2022, p. 6) criticize precisely that such preprocessing and modeling choices are rarely discussed or justified.
    • 
    
  • Crude but useful: from word counts alone, keyness separates "research content" (factors, measurement, validation, causal…) from "course rules" (course, submission, poster, github…). This is a small example of Grimmer & Stewart's first principle, "all models are wrong — but some are useful".
    •

12 · Wrap-up

  
Reading guide: Grimmer & Stewart (2013), Benoit (2020), Baden et al. (2022)

  
In this chapter
About page numbersGrimmer & StewartBenoitBaden et al.Interactive: the English advantageFlashcardsSelf-check


  
How page numbers are cited

  
    
    
  • All three are in W1/papers/ and are the syllabus's three core readings for W1.
    • 
    
  • Grimmer & Stewart (2013): typeset journal PDF; page numbers are journal pages (267–297).
    • 
    
  • Benoit (2020): the version in Singapore Management University's institutional repository (marked pp. 1–55 by the repository), not the SAGE print pagination (461–497); these notes write "repo PDF p. N" (including the repository cover page).
    • 
    
  • Baden et al. (2022): Open Access journal version (CC BY-NC-ND); page numbers are journal pages (1–18).
    • 
  


  

    
Grimmer & Stewart (2013). Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis 21(3): 267–297. Slides 5, 35

    

      
Core claimAutomated text analysis greatly reduces the cost of analyzing large amounts of text, but it has pitfalls: these methods cannot replace careful thought and close reading, and they require extensive, problem-specific validation (abstract, p. 267).

      
Four principles (Table 1, p. 269)(1) All quantitative models of language are wrong — but some are useful; (2) quantitative methods amplify resources and augment humans rather than replace them; (3) there is no globally best method; (4) Validate, Validate, Validate.

      
What principle 1 meansEven linguists do not fully understand how language is generated; models should be judged by whether they accomplish useful social science tasks, not by model fit (pp. 269–270).

      
What principle 4 meansWhen categories are known, show that supervised methods reliably reproduce human coding; validating unsupervised methods is more indirect and combines experimental, substantive and statistical evidence; what must be avoided is "blindly using any method without a validation step" (p. 271).

      
The preprocessing recipeDiscard word order (bag of words) and add bigrams if needed; stemming is a crude approximation of lemmatization; the authors also stress that any step can be, and often should be, modified (p. 272).

      
Link to this weekSlide 5 places this paper at the start of the "Validation" phase: “the four principles — and ‘validate’”. The paper also surveys dictionaries, supervised classification, topics/clustering and scaling, which are the topics of W4–W8.

    

    
Source: W1/papers/Grimmer2013.pdf (Cambridge Core download); doi:10.1093/pan/mps028.

  


  

    
Benoit (2020). Text as Data: An Overview. In Curini & Franzese (eds.), The SAGE Handbook of Research Methods in Political Science and International Relations: 461–497. Slides 12, 36

    

      
Starting pointPolitical science and IR face an "embarrassment of riches" of textual data: legislative debates, manifestos, committee transcripts, speeches, lobbying documents, court opinions and laws are all recorded today, and many are easy to turn into structured data (repo PDF p. 2).

      
Latent vs. manifest characteristicsPolitical science often cares not about the text itself but about the unobservable latent traits it reveals, such as ideology or policy preferences; political communication often cares about manifest characteristics, i.e., the form and content of the communication itself (p. 8).

      
A spectrum of approaches (Table 26.1, p. 12)By degree of automation and "target of concern", from literary, qualitative and hybrid quantitative to purely quantitative. The dividing line is whether the analysis works directly on the text or first extracts features and then analyzes them. (See the PDF for how the table's columns line up; the text-extracted layout is incomplete.)

      
Seven stages (Table 26.2, p. 27)Select texts and define the corpus → convert to a common electronic format → define documents and units of analysis → define and refine features → convert to a quantitative matrix → analyze with appropriate statistical procedures → interpret and report.

      
ConclusionTreating text as data means converting it into features and analyzing patterns in those features, rather than understanding the text directly; this turns text into data that cannot be read directly, but analyzing it can yield insight through structured rules and at a scale impossible to achieve by hand. One driving force is scale (p. 46).

      
Link to this weekThe seven stages are essentially an expanded version of the chain on slide 4; the supplementary lab in chapter 11 does exactly stages 1–5.

    

    
Source: W1/papers/Benoit2020.pdf (Singapore Management University, Institutional Knowledge repository version); doi:10.4135/9781526486387.n29.

  


  

    
Baden, Pipal, Schoonvelde & van der Velden (2022). Three Gaps in Computational Text Analysis Methods for Social Sciences: A Research Agenda. Communication Methods and Measures 16(1): 1–18.

    

      
Research questionWhy is the adoption of computational text analysis methods (CTAM) in the social sciences uneven? The authors argue it is not only that social scientists lack computational skills; often choosing not to use them is reasonable (pp. 1–2).

      
Gap I: Technology before validityCTAM development emphasizes technical and statistical properties over operationalization and measurement validity (from p. 3). Among surveyed authors, 40% saw validity as a major concern and 35% as a minor concern; the preprocessing and modeling choices of (un)supervised CTAM are rarely discussed and almost never justified with existing methodological knowledge (p. 6).

      
Gap II: Specialization before integrationMost tools extract only one kind of textual meaning (e.g., a sentiment score), but social science often needs to measure several internally complex contents at once (e.g., evaluations of specific targets, frames), so tools have to be chained together (from p. 6).

      
Gap III: English before everythingIn top journals, 69% of text-based studies in political science and 59% in communication study only English; cross-lingual comparative studies make up under 16% in communication and 18% in political science; when a second language is added, the share using computational methods falls from 36% to 28% in communication and from 64% to 41% in political science (p. 11).

      
Research agendaSocial scientists are not just tool users and should take part in accumulating methodological knowledge; validation should shift from "predictive accuracy" to "how, and how convincingly, it operationalizes the concept (measurement validity)"; and integrated tools and non-English tools should be developed (from p. 14).

      
Link to this weekEchoes slide 5's "validation never went away"; especially relevant if you do research with Chinese-language or Taiwanese data (W13 covers multilingual data).

    

    
Source: W1/papers/Baden2022.pdf (Taylor & Francis, Open Access); doi:10.1080/19312458.2021.2015574. This paper is not on the slides' reference pages but is listed as a W1 core reading in the syllabus.

13 · Wrap-up

  
Common misconceptions and glossary

  
In this chapter
Common misconceptionsGlossary


  
Common misconceptions (click to see the explanation)

  

    
"This course will teach me transformer architectures and optimization."
No. Slide 11: this is a social science course, not a technical one; the goal is to use these methods to write your own paper.Slide 11

    
"The newer the method, the bigger the contribution."
Catalinac (2016) used LDA from 2003; the contribution was to political science. In application-type research, the protagonists are research design and identification.Slides 6–7

    
"Whatever the model outputs is the result; no need to validate."
Validation is the one requirement that has never gone away; Grimmer & Stewart's fourth principle is Validate, Validate, Validate.Slide 5

    
"I lose points if I don't hand in the lab exercises."
Lab exercises are not graded and do not need to be submitted. But they are your practice ground for the project.Slide 19

    
"If I didn't use AI, I don't need to write a declaration."
Every submission needs a declaration; if you used none, you still write “No generative AI tools were used in the preparation of this assignment.” Submissions without a declaration are not accepted.Slide 29

    
"Submitting to a conference earns the bonus."
The conference bonus requires acceptance; only journals have the rule that a rejected submission also earns +5%, and it must be an SSCI journal, with a confirmation letter and a decision letter.Slides 26–27

    
"Giving the instructor view access on Overleaf counts as submission."
Syllabus §8.1: the instructor must be invited as Editor (can edit); view-only does not count as a submission.

    
"An approved absence means I don't have to do the assignment."
An approved absence or extension does not automatically waive the assignment; the instructor will arrange a reasonable make-up.Slide 30
